# ci-manager-terraform

**Converge a declared terraform root module, and record what it changed.**

A forge-ci `manager` engine.

## Why it exists

Infrastructure a provider holds is declared, never clicked. The engine that
owns it declares one root module and this manager makes the provider hold
what the module says, so a rerun after a wipe rebuilds the same thing and a
second run finds nothing left to do.

## Tools

| Tool | Does |
|---|---|
| `reconcile` | Converge every declared root module and return who owns it. |

## By hand

```sh
echo '{"manager":"terraform","resources":[{"kind":"root-module","name":"home-record","spec":{"dir":"terraform/home-record"}}]}' \
  | ci-manager-terraform reconcile
```

## In a pipeline

```yaml
engines:
  - alias: my-manager
    type: manager
    engine: "forge://github.com/alexandremahdhaoui/forge-ci/cmd/ci-manager-terraform@v0.1.0"
    manager: local
    spec:
      statePath: <string>
```

## Worth knowing

It knows one kind, `root-module`. The resource name is the module's name in
the declaration and `spec.dir` is the directory holding it. The module
declares its own backend and its own variables, so nothing about a provider
or a credential travels through this manager.

A plan answers twice and both answers decide. The exit code says whether
terraform found anything to do. The plan document says what, and the manager
counts every resource change and every output change that is not a no-op and
not a read. A change terraform reads rather than writes is nothing to apply,
so a data source terraform could not resolve at plan time is Kept and never
an endless Did. A pending import is a change even when the resource already
matches the module, because the state gains it and a second run would
otherwise read the same import forever.

The two answers explain different failures, so the manager refuses whenever
they disagree. An exit code saying there is work over a document counting
none, or a document counting work under an exit code saying there is none,
is an error naming both answers and every action the document held. Neither
answer wins, because a manager that picks one and guesses turns an unknown
plan shape into a silent wrong answer, and a wrong answer here stops every
run. A refusal by name gets read and fixed.

Kept means both answers say there is nothing to do. Did means both say there
is, and the apply closed it. A failed init, a failed plan or a failed apply
is an error naming the action and the directory.

A plan terraform could not complete is refused before the two answers are
compared, with the number of deferred changes named. Terraform reports the
completeness of a plan since 1.8, and a plan that defers work carries real
work in a list this manager does not apply, so answering Kept over it would
report a converged module that is not converged.

A dry run initializes and plans exactly as a real run does and answers Kept
either way, with the text saying how many changes it would apply. It applies
nothing. Init writes only the module's own provider cache.

Force applies a plan that holds no change. Only a human asks for it, and it
is the way to reconcile a module whose plan cannot see what a provider did.
It never forces past a plan the two answers disagree on.

There is no delete path. A module dropped from a declaration stays as it is.
It refuses a resource recorded as owned by a different manager.

The credential terraform needs is whatever the module's providers read from
the environment. This engine names none of them, so a module of any provider
runs through it unchanged. Terraform reads them at plan time and this manager
never writes them to state, actions or logs.

Two honest limits. The apply plans again rather than applying the plan the
manager read, so the count in a Did line comes from the earlier plan and a
change landing between the two is applied without being counted. And a forced
run over a plan holding nothing to change says it applied zero planned
changes, which counts the plan rather than naming what the apply did.
